summary: This document defines ways to identify a digital object using the output of a hash function. It specifies a new URI scheme, a way to map such names to HTTP URLs, and binary and human-speakable formats. The names can link strongly to the content, so the object can be checked against its reference.

eli5.summary: Instead of naming a file by where it lives, you name it by its fingerprint. If the fingerprint matches, you know you got the right thing.

questions: how to name things with hashes
what is the ni uri scheme
how to name a file by its hash
subtitle: Standard ways to name a digital object by the output of a hash function, so the name can verify the content.

tldr.problem: Many deployments put hash outputs into identifiers in their own ways, causing interoperability problems, and there is no standard way to check that a retrieved object matches the name used to request it.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the ni URI scheme, a mapping to .well-known HTTP(S) URLs, a URL segment form, a compact binary format and a human-speakable nih URI scheme, all built from an algorithm name and a hash value.
tldr.outcome: A name can carry a strong link to its object, so the object can be authenticated to the same degree as the reference to it. sha-256 is mandatory to implement.

today: RFC 6920 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated according to the metadata.

sections.title: Names Made of Hashes
sections.content:
Identifiers in many protocols already contain values from hash functions, but each deployment includes them in a different way. RFC 6920 defines the Named Information identifier, a set of standard ways to use hash function outputs in names.

The RFC lists several uses. Hash outputs can make URIs unique or hard to guess. Constrained devices need compact binary forms. People may need to read a value out in a voice call. In-network storage needs location-independent names, and clients want to verify that what they got matches the name they asked for. The RFC calls that last property name-data integrity.

A name names a resource. The entity that dereferences it must already know how to locate the resource.
sections.eli5: A fingerprint name is like a sticker that describes exactly what is inside a box. You can open any box that looks right and check if it matches the sticker.

sections.title: Hashes Are What Count
sections.content:
When comparing two names, an implementation MUST consider only the digest algorithm and the digest value. Authority fields and parameters are ignored. Two hashes are identical, regardless of encoding, if the decoded hashes use the same algorithm, have the same length and have the same binary value.

The sha-256 algorithm is mandatory to implement: implementations MUST be able to generate, send, accept and process names based on it. They MAY support other algorithms.

Truncated hashes MAY be supported, but the name MUST indicate it, with strings such as sha-256-32 for a 32-bit truncation. The leftmost N bits are used. The RFC warns that a 32-bit truncated hash is essentially useless for security, and that very few applications using names with less than 100-bit hashes will have useful security properties.

When the input is a public key, the hash SHOULD be computed over an X.509 SubjectPublicKeyInfo structure. Apart from that case, the RFC leaves the hash input to other specifications.
sections.eli5: Only the fingerprint matters when checking if two names are the same. A short, smudged fingerprint is not the same as a full one.

sections.title: The ni URI Format
sections.content:
A Named Information (ni) URI has the shape ni://authority/alg;val?query. The authority is optional and has no default. The alg is a digest algorithm name from the IANA registry. The val MUST be the digest value encoded with base64url with no = padding. The value is the hash of the object bytes that would be returned when the URI is dereferenced, unless the algorithm defines another input.

Names with and without an authority differ syntactically, but all refer to the same object if and only if the digest algorithm, length and value are the same. Checking the integrity of the URI-to-resource mapping is OPTIONAL.

Optional query parameters are tag=value pairs. One is defined here: ct, the MIME Content Type. Implementations MUST support parsing it. If the client is sensitive to Content Type, the name has ct, and the retrieval protocol gives a Content Type, a mismatch SHOULD be handled as a potential security error. Implementations SHOULD support name-data integrity validation for at least application/octet-stream.
sections.eli5: An ni name is written as a label with the kind of fingerprint, a semicolon, and then the fingerprint itself in letters and numbers.

sections.title: .well-known URLs and URL Segments
sections.content:
An ni name can be mapped to an HTTP or HTTPS URL using the .well-known URI mechanism and an ni suffix. The name ni://n-authority/alg;val?query-string becomes http://h-authority/.well-known/ni/alg/val?query-string. If the ni name has an authority, the h-authority MUST be the same. If not, it MAY be derived from the application context, such as the origin of a web page.

Because the .well-known space is not meant for general retrieval, a client will often get a 3xx redirect and MUST be able to handle it. Whether to use http or https is left to the application. There is no guarantee that the object is available at the mapped URL, but a retriever can check whether returned content matches the name.

The alg;val pair can also be placed as a segment in the path, query or fragment of an existing URL. Clients MUST NOT assume that such a URL was produced by this specification.
sections.eli5: If a program cannot read ni names, you can rewrite the name as an ordinary web address that a browser can follow.

sections.title: The Binary Format
sections.content:
Where space matters, a binary name has two fields: a header and the hash value. The header is a 2-bit Res field followed by a Suite ID. Res is reserved, MUST be zero and is ignored on receipt. The Suite ID identifies the hash algorithm and truncation length from the IANA registry.

A hash value truncated to 120 bits gives an overall name of 128 bits, which suits protocols that use 128-bit identifiers.
sections.eli5: The binary format is a short code that says which fingerprint method was used, followed by the fingerprint, with no extra letters.

sections.title: Human-Speakable nih Names
sections.content:
The nih (Named Information for Humans) URI scheme is for reading a hash over, for example, a phone call. base64url mixes upper and lower case, which is easy to confuse when spoken, so nih uses lowercase hex. It leaves out the authority and the query string.

The form is nih:alg;sepval;checkdigit. Hyphen separators MAY be inserted in the hash value to make it easier to read, typically in groups of four or six characters. The optional check digit MUST be computed with Luhn's mod N algorithm with N=16, over the hex value with the separators removed. The alg field MAY be a decimal Suite ID, such as 3 for sha-256-120.

The RFC's usage example has Alice read out the nih form of her server's public key name to Bob, who types it into an admin tool to regenerate the ni URI and can then more safely accept her node's signature.
sections.eli5: An nih name is a fingerprint written in a way that is easy to say aloud, with a check number at the end to catch mistakes in hearing.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The RFC registers the ni and nih URI schemes as Permanent, and the ni suffix in the Well-Known URI registry. It also creates two registries, both with Expert Review for new entries.

The Named Information Hash Algorithm Registry has a suite ID (empty or 0 to 63), a name string, a truncation length, a reference and a status of current or deprecated. The Designated Expert SHOULD NOT accept algorithms whose untruncated hash is considered weak for collisions. Suite ID 32 is reserved for compatibility with IPv6 addresses such as ORCHIDs. The Named Information URI Parameter Definitions registry initially holds just ct.
sections.eli5: The new name styles and the list of allowed fingerprint methods are written in official lists that others can add to with expert approval.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
No secret is needed to generate or verify a name, so a name only provides evidence of integrity, and only as good as the integrity of the name itself. Names also do not protect confidentiality: an attacker might find the content from a search engine, or guess a highly formatted object and check the digest.

A weak hash function would compromise integrity, which is why only SHA-256-based suites were added initially. Shorter hashes give less security. A name with a 32-bit truncated hash is not the same as one with the full 256 bits, even if one is a prefix of the other, so the algorithm, length and value must all match.

An authority in an ni URI implies nothing about the relationship between the domain owner and the content, and developers MUST NOT assume one. An ni URI with non-base64 characters, whitespace or other non-conforming strings MUST NOT be treated as matching any other ni URI.
sections.eli5: A fingerprint tells you a box matches its label, but it does not keep the box secret, and a tiny partial fingerprint can match many different boxes.
